Osmolality increases as there are more particles in solution, so more potential to pull water across the membrane. ADH levels increases to constrict the afferent arteriole, reducing the GFR but increasing the filtration of water at the glomerulus. This dilutes the high concentration of salt.  Salt or plasma solute concentration is directly proportional to GFR. The higher the concentration of solute/salt the more water is filtered (higher GFR). The more water is filtered the more dilute the plasma becomes (decreasing plasma osmolality)  The kidney cannot adjust to every change, only small changes are compensated. In this situation there is too much salt being taken in.  The body has to excrete some of it. This could be done through urination or sweating. However, if there is no way for the body to get rid of the excess salt then the body will have to compensate by retaining water. This would cause an increase in blood volume which would dilute the plasma osmolality.  To counteract this, the hypothalamus would sense the increased blood volume and release ADH which would act on the collecting duct of the nephron to reduce the amount of water reabsorbed into the systemic circulation. The more water that is reabsorbed, the higher the osmolality will become.  The reason why the ADH levels increase is because it is a hormone released when there is a decrease in blood volume, which in turn causes the kidneys to increase the reabsorption of water.  It is important to note that the kidneys respond two seconds later than the thirst mechanism. This means that the body will continue to drink until the osmolality reaches equilibrium. It is broken down by the enzyme dipeptidyl peptidase IV (DDP4). GIP increases insulin production and decreases glucagon production in beta cells and increases insulin sensitivity. It is not as effective as GLP-1. Both of these work to mimic the normal insulin response. Sulphonylureas such as gliclazide act to increase insulin secretion. They are used when natural incretins are not working properly. They may be used with Type 2 diabetics who are overweight or obese because they cause weight gain. This would not be ideal in all cases. Alpha Glucosidase Inhibitors such as acarbose prevent the breakdown of starch into maltose and glucose. They slow the rate at which glucose enters the bloodstream after eating. They are not very effective and do not cause any weight gain. They are used alongside other treatments. Fibrates reduce triglycerides in the blood. Statins reduce cholesterol in the blood. Omega-3 reduces triglycerides in the blood. All of these drugs are used in conjunction with lifestyle changes. Erb-Duchenne palsy is also known as Erb's palsy or brachial plexus injury. It is a condition where the arm nerve may be damaged near where it enters the spinal column. Symptoms include numbness and weakness of the arm due to injury to the upper group of the arm's main nerves. This usually affects the shoulder, elbow, and wrist. The muscles of the hand are usually not affected. Erb–Duchenne paralysis results from injury to the superior trunk and posterior divisions of the arm nerve. This injury causes paralysis of the muscles of the deltoid, teres minor, infraspinatus, and serratus anterior. It also causes loss of sensation over the lateral deltoid region of the skin. In severe cases, the radial pulse may be diminished or absent. Classically, the hand takes on a "claw" shape, with flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joints and extension at the proximal interphalangeal joints. Patients may also have reduced sensation over the medial deltoid region of skin. This condition may result from shoulder dystocia during labor or trauma to the neck. Acrosome reaction occurs before or during sperm entry into the egg, whereas the cortical reaction occurs afterward. The two are not interchangeable. They are both important events in fertilization. The acrosome reaction involves the exocytosis of the contents of the sperm’s acrosome, which includes a number of enzymes, including hyaluronidase, proteases (e.g., phospholipases, trypsin-like serine proteases, and cysteine proteases), and other substances. These substances help the sperm penetrate the egg’s outer layers and allow it to enter the egg’s cytoplasm. The cortical reaction involves the release of enzymes from granules that lie just beneath the egg’s plasma membrane. The cortical reaction is thought to be triggered by the fusion of the plasma membrane of the sperm and the egg as well as the acidification of the egg’s cytoplasm caused by the activation of the sperm’s plasma membrane. The cortical reaction produces a thick gel around the egg, making it difficult for additional sperm to bind to the egg. It also helps strengthen the corona radiata surrounding the egg, which prevents polyspermy (the simultaneous fertilization of multiple eggs). The timing of these events varies between species but typically occur within seconds of each other. In humans, the acrosome reaction occurs about one minute before the cortical reaction. The cortical reaction appears to be more important than the acrosome reaction in determining whether fertilization will succeed. If successful fertilization does not occur quickly enough after insemination, then there may not be enough time for both reactions to take place before degenerative changes begin occurring inside the egg. Apert's syndrome - Characterised by craniofacial anomalies such as widely spaced eyes, prominent lower jaw and underdeveloped nasal bridge. Also characterised by webbed fingers and toes, and congenital heart defects. Edward's syndrome - Correct answer. This is also known as Trisomy 18, which usually results from meiotic non-disjunction. Symptoms include growth retardation, microcephaly (small head), hypotonia (decreased muscle tone), clenched hands, arthrogryposis (multiple joint contractures) and other abnormalities. Down's syndrome - Also known as trisomy 21. This occurs when there are three copies of chromosome 21 instead of two, causing developmental delays, mild intellectual disability, and distinctive facial features such as upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, small ears, large tongue, low set ears, smooth skin, and white spot on neck. Klinefelter's syndrome - Revealed by karyotyping to be XXY, this condition causes primary hypogonadism, tall stature, breast tissue formation, infertility, and reduced fertility. Patau's syndrome - Also known as trisomy 13, this is caused by either a diploid egg cell or triploid sperm. It is the third most common autosomal trisomy, occurring in approximately 1/5000 births. Symptoms include severe developmental delay, structural abnormalities, and various degrees of growth retardation. The majority of patients die within the first year of life. Meningitis is inflammation of the protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord. Inflammation of the layers surrounding the brain is called encephalitis. Bacterial causes include gram positive bacteria such as streptococci, staphylococci or meningitis, and gram negative bacteria such as Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria meningitidis. Symptoms of bacterial meningitis include fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, seizures, confusion and coma. Lumbar puncture is the gold standard diagnostic test for meningitis because it allows you to look for the presence of microbes, white blood cells and protein in the CSF. The pressure of CSF should also be measured. If the pressure is too high, you must be careful when performing the procedure. The normal pressure is 5-20cm/H20. Glucose may be low due to overwhelming infection, or increased due to stress response. Protein levels will be raised due to inflammation. WBCs >90% polymorphs (PMNs) = bacterial. It is given before the antibiotics so that they can reach the site of infection.  Case 6 - Microbiology of Infectious Diseases lecture.
